claims.text: At elevated temperature, the multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy forms a protective oxide film.
The oxide film is heterogeneous and develops non-uniformly on the alloy's constituent phases.
The protective film is a spinel-type oxide or a functionally similar oxide.
The oxide film is especially discontinuous at interdendritic or eutectic phase boundaries.
Mechanical wear repeatedly removes the elevated-temperature oxide film.
Wear removes the oxide preferentially at phase boundaries.
Removal of the oxide exposes fresh, chemically active metal that then corrodes rapidly.
Localized corrosion undermines the mechanical integrity of phase boundaries.
Corrosion-induced weakening of phase boundaries accelerates subsequent wear.
Film removal, localized corrosion, and accelerated wear form a self-amplifying positive-feedback cycle.
Combined wear-corrosion damage will exceed the sum of damage measured in isolated wear-only and corrosion-only tests.
Relative to inert-atmosphere wear, simultaneous corrosion will increase the wear rate through corrosion-induced softening or boundary weakening.
Relative to static corrosion, simultaneous wear will increase pitting or corrosion rates by disrupting the protective film.
The proposed regime is 500–900 °C under reciprocating or sliding contact in an oxidizing or chloride-containing environment.
The synergistic mechanism requires a temperature high enough for oxide formation and rapid oxidation kinetics.
The synergistic mechanism requires a sufficiently oxidizing or corrosive environment, potentially including chloride ions.
The wear load must be sufficient to remove the oxide periodically but below the level causing corrosion-independent catastrophic failure.
A three-arm comparison of simultaneous wear-corrosion, inert wear-only, and no-wear corrosion-only conditions can distinguish the proposed synergy.
Mass loss, wear-track depth, pit depth and density, oxide continuity, and phase-boundary degradation are measurable discriminating outcomes.
Failure to observe either super-additive total damage or oxide removal at phase boundaries falsifies the hypothesis.
